events.type: media report about the largest customer / largest project (Oracle, Project Jupiter)
events.summary: Bloomberg reported that Oracle has trucked compressed natural gas to at least two data-center sites while waiting for pipelines (a site outside Salt Lake City for more than a year, and initial work at the campus it is building for OpenAI in Shackelford County, Texas), and that it is weighing trucked gas for Project Jupiter in Dona Ana County, New Mexico. Jupiter is meant to run on Bloom fuel cells (Oracle said in April: up to 2.45 GW in an on-site microgrid) but still has no gas supply. Energy Transfer's Green Chile pipeline now targets 2027-02-01, slipped from 2026-08-15. Trucked gas 'could allow the initial phases to operate before the pipeline... begins service'. An East Daley Analytics analyst estimated delivered compressed gas costs roughly four times the price of gas at a major pipeline hub. Oracle's only quoted statement praised VoltaGrid (a rival on-site gas-power provider): 'Shoutout to the Voltagrid team for finding cost-effective power solutions to ensure our customers can access OCI capacity on schedule.' Investing.com (2026-10-08, 1:22 PM) wrote that Bloom shares 'dropped more than 7.5%' following the report. No comment from Bloom was found. The Bloomberg original was not accessed (paywall); details come from two independent rewrites plus local New Mexico reporting.
events.why_it_matters: Jupiter is Bloom's biggest single project, and gas supply is its bottleneck. The report re-confirms the February 2027 pipeline date (no new slip) and adds a possible bridge (trucked gas) that could let early phases start sooner, but at roughly 4x the fuel cost. The market read it as bad news on the day; the content itself does not change the contract.

A report questioning OpenAI's revenue hits that chain at its source; higher yields also hurt expensive growth stocks like Bloom (about 108x expected profit per the thesis file).

products.name: Bloom Energy Server (solid-oxide fuel cell power system) for Oracle data centers / Project Jupiter
products.what_it_is: Refrigerator-sized boxes that turn natural gas into electricity through a chemical reaction instead of burning it, installed on the customer's site.
products.analogy: Like a home generator that never runs its engine: gas goes in, electricity comes out through a battery-like reaction, so it is quieter and cleaner, but it still needs a steady gas supply, the way a car needs a fuel station nearby.
products.buyers: AI data-center builders (Oracle is the biggest named one), and increasingly utilities (Ameren plans 500 MW per a Barclays note, tier 3, already in news log).
products.how_it_works: Natural gas (from a pipeline or, as a stop-gap, trucked as compressed gas) feeds the fuel-cell stacks; the systems sit next to the data center in a 'microgrid' (a small, self-contained power network), so the site does not wait years for a grid connection. Without gas supply the boxes cannot run, which is why the Jupiter pipeline matters.
products.sales: Q2 2026 product revenue $935.4m (+215.4% y/y) of $1,065.4m total; service $69.0m, installation $51.0m, electricity $9.9m. Oracle: intends to procure up to 2.8 GW, 1.2 GW contracted (2026-04-13). Jupiter: up to 2.45 GW (Oracle, April 2026). Megawatts shipped and backlog: not disclosed in the Q2 release. Revenue from Oracle specifically: not disclosed (proxy: the 1.2 GW contracted figure).
products.sales_source: Bloom Q2 2026 results, 2026-07-28 (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001664703/000162828026050150/ex991_q226financialresults.htm); Bloom-Oracle press release, 2026-04-13 (https://www.bloomenergy.com/?p=21516); Yahoo Finance/Blockspace, 2026-10-09 for the 2.45 GW Jupiter figure
products.stage: Shipping at scale; Jupiter installation waiting on gas supply (pipeline target 2027-02-01; trucked gas under consideration).
products.size_for_company: Product sales were about 88% of Q2 revenue ($935.4m / $1,065.4m, arithmetic). Oracle's 2.8 GW intention is large relative to Bloom's business, but its revenue share is not disclosed.
products.competition: Gas engines and turbines from on-site providers (e.g. VoltaGrid, which Oracle praised in its 2026-10-08 statement), grid power, batteries; nuclear and utilities (Vistra, Constellation, Oklo) for longer-term supply.
products.why_investors_care: Speed to power is Bloom's selling point; if gas cannot reach the site, the speed advantage shrinks. Trucked gas could keep early phases on schedule but at higher fuel cost.
products.watch_next: Whether Oracle actually trucks gas to Jupiter; any further pipeline slip beyond 2027-02-01; Bloom's Q3 call comments on Oracle, Jupiter timing and backlog.
